title: Organic Chemistry III
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Organic Chemistry III curriculum: structure, nomenclature, and reactions of carbonyl compounds (aldehydes/ketones), carboxylic acids and derivatives, amines, aromatic substitution chemistry, stereochemistry, and an introduction to heterocyclic compounds -- building further than the alkane/alkene/alcohol-focused Organic Chemistry I/II. Detailed reaction mechanisms are left to the dedicated CHM306 Organic Reaction Mechanisms course.

questions.question: In IUPAC nomenclature, the suffix used for a ketone functional group is:
questions.correct_answer: -one
questions.explanation: Ketones are named with the suffix '-one' (e.g. propan-2-one/acetone), indicating a carbonyl group flanked by two carbon substituents.

questions.question: Aldehydes are generally more reactive toward nucleophilic addition than ketones mainly because:
options: Aldehydes have two alkyl groups shielding the carbonyl carbon
The carbonyl carbon in aldehydes is less sterically hindered and less electron-donated to (only one alkyl/H group), making it more electrophilic
questions.correct_answer: The carbonyl carbon in aldehydes is less sterically hindered and less electron-donated to (only one alkyl/H group), making it more electrophilic
questions.explanation: With only one alkyl group (and a hydrogen) attached, aldehydes are less sterically hindered and less electron-rich at the carbonyl carbon than ketones, making them more susceptible to nucleophilic attack.

questions.question: The Tollens' test (silver mirror test) is used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones because:
options: Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (Ag(NH3)2+) to metallic silver, forming a mirror, while ketones generally do not react
Ketones always form a silver mirror
Both aldehydes and ketones give identical results
questions.correct_answer: Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent (Ag(NH3)2+) to metallic silver, forming a mirror, while ketones generally do not react
questions.explanation: Aldehydes are readily oxidised to carboxylic acids, reducing the diamminesilver(I) complex to metallic silver (the 'mirror'); ketones lack this easily oxidisable hydrogen and do not respond under mild conditions.

questions.question: The product of a Grignard reagent (RMgX) reacting with formaldehyde (HCHO), after aqueous workup, is:
questions.correct_answer: A primary alcohol
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde has only a hydrogen and oxygen on the carbonyl carbon, so nucleophilic addition of RMgX followed by aqueous workup gives a primary alcohol (RCH2OH).

questions.question: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols mainly because:
options: The carboxylate anion formed after deprotonation is resonance-stabilised over two equivalent oxygen atoms
Carboxylic acids have no oxygen atoms
Carboxylic acids cannot lose a proton
questions.correct_answer: The carboxylate anion formed after deprotonation is resonance-stabilised over two equivalent oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: Loss of the O-H proton from a carboxylic acid gives a carboxylate ion whose negative charge is delocalised equally between two oxygens, providing significant stabilisation that alkoxide ions (from alcohols) lack.

questions.question: Which of the following carboxylic acid derivatives is generally the LEAST reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
questions.correct_answer: Amide
questions.explanation: Reactivity order for acyl substitution is acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, reflecting the leaving-group ability and resonance donation of the substituent attached to the carbonyl; the amide nitrogen's strong resonance donation makes it least reactive.

questions.question: Fischer esterification is the acid-catalysed reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form:
questions.correct_answer: An ester and water
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification, catalysed by a strong acid (e.g. H2SO4), condenses a carboxylic acid and an alcohol into an ester, releasing water; the reaction is reversible (equilibrium-controlled).

questions.question: Saponification is the base-catalysed hydrolysis of an ester (e.g. a triglyceride) that produces:
options: A carboxylate salt (soap) and an alcohol
questions.correct_answer: A carboxylate salt (soap) and an alcohol
questions.explanation: Saponification with NaOH/KOH hydrolyses the ester bonds of fats/oils irreversibly, producing glycerol (the alcohol) and carboxylate salts, which are soaps.

questions.question: Amines are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on:
options: The number of carbon atoms in the molecule
The number of carbon (alkyl/aryl) groups directly bonded to the nitrogen atom
The molecular weight of the amine
Whether the amine is aromatic or not
questions.correct_answer: The number of carbon (alkyl/aryl) groups directly bonded to the nitrogen atom
questions.explanation: Unlike alcohols (classified by the carbon bearing OH), amines are classified by how many carbon groups are attached directly to nitrogen: one (primary), two (secondary), or three (tertiary).

questions.question: Aniline (phenylamine) is a weaker base than a typical aliphatic amine such as methylamine because:
options: The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available to accept a proton
Aniline has more alkyl groups than methylamine
questions.correct_answer: The nitrogen lone pair in aniline is delocalised into the benzene ring, making it less available to accept a proton
questions.explanation: Resonance delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair into the aromatic pi system stabilises aniline but reduces the lone pair's availability for protonation, making it considerably less basic than aliphatic amines.

questions.question: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a substituent such as -OH or -NH2 on a benzene ring is classified as an activating, ortho/para-directing group mainly because it:
options: Withdraws electron density from the ring inductively and by resonance
Donates electron density into the ring by resonance, increasing electron density most at the ortho and para positions
Has no effect on ring reactivity
questions.correct_answer: Donates electron density into the ring by resonance, increasing electron density most at the ortho and para positions
questions.explanation: Lone-pair-bearing substituents like -OH and -NH2 donate electron density into the ring via resonance, strongly activating it toward electrophiles and directing substitution to ortho/para positions where the resonance structures place negative charge.

questions.question: A nitro group (-NO2) on a benzene ring is a deactivating, meta-directing substituent because it:
options: Donates electrons into the ring by resonance
Strongly withdraws electron density from the ring both inductively and by resonance, destabilising ortho/para intermediates more than meta
Has no electronic effect on the ring
questions.correct_answer: Strongly withdraws electron density from the ring both inductively and by resonance, destabilising ortho/para intermediates more than meta
questions.explanation: The electron-withdrawing nitro group destabilises the arenium ion intermediate most severely when positive charge would fall on the ring carbon bearing it (ortho/para attack), so substitution is directed to the meta position, and the ring overall is deactivated.

questions.question: Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene, using an alkyl halide and an AlCl3 catalyst, suffers from the practical limitation that:
options: It cannot occur on any aromatic ring
The alkylbenzene product is more activated (electron-rich) than benzene itself, favouring polyalkylation, and carbocation rearrangements can occur
It only works with strongly deactivated rings
questions.correct_answer: The alkylbenzene product is more activated (electron-rich) than benzene itself, favouring polyalkylation, and carbocation rearrangements can occur
questions.explanation: Because alkyl groups are activating, the monoalkylated product reacts faster than benzene, often giving polyalkylated mixtures; the intermediate carbocation can also rearrange to a more stable one, complicating product control.

questions.question: A chiral carbon (stereocentre) is defined as a carbon atom bonded to:
options: Three identical groups and one different
questions.correct_answer: Four different groups
questions.explanation: A stereocentre has four distinct substituents, meaning the two possible spatial arrangements are non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers).

questions.question: The (R) and (S) descriptors in the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog system are assigned by:
options: Ranking the four substituents on a stereocentre by priority (based on atomic number) and observing whether priority decreases clockwise (R) or anticlockwise (S) with the lowest-priority group pointing away from the viewer
Measuring the optical rotation with a polarimeter
Counting the number of carbon atoms in the molecule
questions.correct_answer: Ranking the four substituents on a stereocentre by priority (based on atomic number) and observing whether priority decreases clockwise (R) or anticlockwise (S) with the lowest-priority group pointing away from the viewer
questions.explanation: CIP rules assign priority by atomic number (and further tie-breaking rules) at each substituent; viewing with the lowest priority group away from the observer, clockwise decreasing priority is R (rectus), anticlockwise is S (sinister).

questions.question: Diastereomers differ from enantiomers in that diastereomers are:
options: Non-superimposable mirror images of each other
Stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images of each other, and generally have different physical properties (m.p., b.p., solubility)
questions.correct_answer: Stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images of each other, and generally have different physical properties (m.p., b.p., solubility)
questions.explanation: Diastereomers arise in molecules with two or more stereocentres where not all centres are inverted between the two isomers; unlike enantiomers (identical physical properties except optical rotation direction), diastereomers have genuinely different physical properties.

questions.question: A racemic mixture consists of:
options: Equal amounts of both enantiomers of a chiral compound, resulting in zero net optical rotation
questions.correct_answer: Equal amounts of both enantiomers of a chiral compound, resulting in zero net optical rotation
questions.explanation: A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers is optically inactive overall because the equal and opposite rotations of the two enantiomers cancel out.

questions.question: Meso compounds, such as meso-tartaric acid, are achiral despite having stereocentres because:
options: They have no stereocentres at all
They possess an internal plane of symmetry (or improper axis), making the molecule superimposable on its own mirror image
They cannot be drawn with a Fischer projection
questions.correct_answer: They possess an internal plane of symmetry (or improper axis), making the molecule superimposable on its own mirror image
questions.explanation: A meso compound has multiple stereocentres but an internal mirror plane that makes the molecule identical to its own mirror image, so it is achiral and optically inactive despite the presence of stereocentres.

questions.question: Furan, pyrrole, and thiophene are five-membered heterocyclic compounds that are all aromatic because:
options: They each have a heteroatom whose lone pair contributes to a cyclic, continuously conjugated system of 6 pi electrons obeying Hückel's rule
questions.correct_answer: They each have a heteroatom whose lone pair contributes to a cyclic, continuously conjugated system of 6 pi electrons obeying Hückel's rule
questions.explanation: In furan, pyrrole, and thiophene, one lone pair on the heteroatom (O, N, or S) occupies a p-orbital and joins the ring's conjugated pi system, giving 6 delocalised pi electrons and satisfying Hückel's (4n+2) rule for aromaticity.

questions.question: Pyridine, a six-membered nitrogen heterocycle, differs from pyrrole in basicity because in pyridine:
options: The nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic pi system, so it is available to accept a proton, making pyridine more basic than pyrrole
The lone pair is fully delocalised into the ring, exactly like pyrrole
questions.correct_answer: The nitrogen lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, not part of the aromatic pi system, so it is available to accept a proton, making pyridine more basic than pyrrole
questions.explanation: Pyridine's nitrogen contributes one electron (not its lone pair) to the aromatic sextet, leaving its lone pair free in an sp2 orbital for protonation, unlike pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair, which is committed to the aromatic pi system and largely unavailable, making pyrrole far less basic.

questions.question: The aldol reaction involves the base- or acid-catalysed addition of an enolate (from one carbonyl compound) to the carbonyl carbon of another, producing:
questions.correct_answer: A beta-hydroxy carbonyl compound (aldol)
questions.explanation: In the aldol reaction, an enolate nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of another aldehyde/ketone, giving a beta-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone, which can further dehydrate to an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound.

questions.question: Which of these functional groups, when the parent chain contains both a carboxylic acid and an alcohol group, takes priority for the principal characteristic group in IUPAC naming?
options: The alcohol (named as the parent, suffix -ol)
The carboxylic acid (named as the parent, suffix -oic acid, with the OH cited as 'hydroxy-' prefix)
Both are named as suffixes simultaneously
questions.correct_answer: The carboxylic acid (named as the parent, suffix -oic acid, with the OH cited as 'hydroxy-' prefix)
questions.explanation: IUPAC seniority order places carboxylic acids above alcohols, so the acid is named as the suffix and any hydroxyl group is cited as a 'hydroxy-' substituent prefix, e.g. 3-hydroxybutanoic acid.

questions.question: Decarboxylation of a beta-keto acid (a carboxylic acid with a ketone at the beta position) occurs readily on mild heating because:
options: It proceeds through a cyclic six-membered transition state, transferring the acidic proton and expelling CO2 to form an enol, which tautomerises to the ketone
Decarboxylation requires strong acid catalysis at very high temperature only
questions.correct_answer: It proceeds through a cyclic six-membered transition state, transferring the acidic proton and expelling CO2 to form an enol, which tautomerises to the ketone
questions.explanation: Beta-keto acids undergo facile thermal decarboxylation via a cyclic transition state involving the carbonyl oxygen, distinguishing them from simple carboxylic acids, which require harsher conditions to lose CO2.

questions.question: The Hofmann elimination of a quaternary ammonium hydroxide gives predominantly the LESS substituted (Hofmann) alkene product because:
options: The bulky leaving group/base favours removal of the more accessible, less hindered beta-hydrogen
Quaternary ammonium salts cannot undergo elimination
Only tertiary amines can be eliminated
questions.correct_answer: The bulky leaving group/base favours removal of the more accessible, less hindered beta-hydrogen
questions.explanation: Because the trimethylamine leaving group is bulky, steric factors favour deprotonation at the least hindered beta-carbon, giving the less-substituted (Hofmann) alkene as the major product, in contrast to the more-substituted (Zaitsev) product typically favoured in E1 reactions.

questions.question: Acid anhydrides are typically prepared from two molecules of a carboxylic acid, or more practically from a carboxylic acid and an acid chloride, because anhydride formation:
options: Involves loss of water (or HCl, when using an acid chloride) between two carboxyl-containing molecules to form the C-O-C anhydride linkage
Produces an amide as the only product
questions.correct_answer: Involves loss of water (or HCl, when using an acid chloride) between two carboxyl-containing molecules to form the C-O-C anhydride linkage
questions.explanation: Anhydrides contain two acyl groups joined through a single oxygen; they are commonly made by condensing two carboxylic acids (removing water) or by reacting an acid chloride with a carboxylate/acid (releasing HCl).

questions.question: The Gabriel synthesis is a method for preparing primary amines that is valued because it:
options: Avoids over-alkylation (a common problem with direct alkyl halide + ammonia reactions) by using phthalimide as a protected nitrogen nucleophile
questions.correct_answer: Avoids over-alkylation (a common problem with direct alkyl halide + ammonia reactions) by using phthalimide as a protected nitrogen nucleophile
questions.explanation: The Gabriel synthesis alkylates potassium phthalimide with an alkyl halide, then hydrolyses/hydrazinolyses the product to release a clean primary amine, sidestepping the polyalkylation problem of directly alkylating ammonia.

questions.question: Carboxylic acids exhibit unusually high boiling points relative to alcohols/aldehydes of similar molar mass mainly because:
options: Two carboxylic acid molecules readily form a cyclic dimer held together by two strong hydrogen bonds
questions.correct_answer: Two carboxylic acid molecules readily form a cyclic dimer held together by two strong hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids commonly exist as hydrogen-bonded dimers (via both C=O···H-O interactions), effectively doubling the molecular mass in the liquid/vapour phase and raising the boiling point well above comparable alcohols.

questions.question: Enamine formation results from the reaction of a ketone or aldehyde with:
options: A primary amine, forming an imine instead
A secondary amine, followed by loss of water to give a C=C-N system
questions.correct_answer: A secondary amine, followed by loss of water to give a C=C-N system
questions.explanation: Secondary amines cannot form a stable imine (no N-H left to lose as the second equivalent of water), so instead a proton is lost from the alpha-carbon, giving an enamine (C=C-NR2) after dehydration.

questions.question: In the Cannizzaro reaction, a non-enolisable aldehyde (one with no alpha-hydrogens, e.g. benzaldehyde) reacts with concentrated base to give:
options: A mixture of the corresponding alcohol and carboxylate salt, via disproportionation (simultaneous oxidation and reduction)
questions.correct_answer: A mixture of the corresponding alcohol and carboxylate salt, via disproportionation (simultaneous oxidation and reduction)
questions.explanation: Lacking an alpha-hydrogen for aldol chemistry, non-enolisable aldehydes undergo base-mediated disproportionation: one molecule is reduced to the alcohol while another is oxidised to the carboxylate.
